body:
Three plan-families are now on the table, each attached to a preferred diagnosis: the account bets on ambiguity and prescribes specification; the objection weakens the bet by showing the same evidence fits renegotiation or legitimacy readings, and that the account's test cannot tell them apart; the rival adds an axis nobody else had — whether the flat is a unit with obligations or three private lives sharing fixtures — and prescribes conversations about that. A fourth plan would be the wrong contribution. What is missing is not another arrangement but a way to choose among the three that exist, and the person holding the evidence needed for that choice is you.

All three artifacts reasoned from the problem statement, which is genuinely thin as a shared text. But you were in the arguments. The cheapest next step is retrospective, not prospective, and none of the artifacts took it.

Take the last two disputes you remember clearly — recent ones, where you trust your memory of the wording — and sort them by what the fight was actually about, in the words used:

- "That's not what I said" / "I thought you meant by the weekend" — a dispute about what the agreement meant. Supports the ambiguity reading.
- "I agreed when my shifts were different" / "things have changed" — a dispute about whether the terms still bind. Supports the renegotiation reading.
- "Why is it always you deciding?" / "fine, whatever" — a dispute about who has standing to raise or enforce. Supports the legitimacy reading.
- Silence, leaving the room, agreeing and then not showing up — a conversation that never got to be about the chore, because the conversation itself was the thing refused. Supports the form or household-identity readings.

The objection's p1 named the first three axes; the rival's r4 named the fourth territory. My addition is only that this is runnable tonight, from memory, and that the result chooses among the plans rather than adjudicating them. If disputes cluster on the ambiguity row, the account's plan stands and the objection's own concession (o4) applies — if you genuinely cannot reconstruct what was agreed, ambiguity is the plainest reading. If they cluster on renegotiation, the account's best column ("what happens when someone can't") should become the main one; renegotiation clauses matter more than done-ness criteria. If they cluster on legitimacy, no document helps, because documents will be read as enforcement; the work is on standing — who raises things, how, and whether it is always the same person.

Classify by wording, not by gist — gist is where your current interpretation does its rewriting. There is a free cross-check: the other non-withdrawing flatmate classifies the same disputes privately, and you compare notes. But compare notes only; do not let it become a joint front, for a reason I'll give below.

The objection asked (u1) that the readings sit side by side with a probe designed to distinguish them. That request is granted, and the rival supplied the best prospective observation: r7 — when a proposal is made, does the withdrawing friend engage with its content or pull back from the proposal itself? Adopt it. It needs a low-coercion vehicle, since you cannot observe reaction-to-proposal without making one. The vehicle I'd use is a self-assuming offer: in the one-to-one conversation the account already recommends (step 4, which all three artifacts support in some form), make exactly one small, revocable offer that requires nothing from them — "what if the bin just became mine on Thursdays, would that help or annoy you?" — and listen. Relief plus continued distance elsewhere suggests the form or privacy readings. Engaging with content once the pressure is off suggests ambiguity. Resentment at being offered something suggests legitimacy. "It's not about the bin" is the most useful answer of all, because it opens the actual topic.

Three revisions to the rival, whose axis I accept. First, don't ask the identity question directly. "Do you see this flat as a unit or three private lives?" is a large abstract question, and the rival's own r4 says the avoidance tracks the form and stakes of conversations; a direct version reproduces the form. Probe the identity reading behaviorally and let it be inferred. Second, the rival's truce arrangements have a fixture problem. Zones work for private areas, and private areas are rarely what's disputed; the recurring items — bins, bathroom, kitchen surfaces — are shared or contiguous, which is exactly where zone logic breaks down, because the sink is in everyone's zone or nobody's. The truce that actually matches a privacy reading on shared fixtures is a tolerance agreement: an explicit mutual decision to live with a full bin for a day rather than audit it. Note what that costs — it is the unit-reading flatmates who give up something visible. A truce that only restrains the withdrawing friend's obligations is not a truce. Third, keep the rival's r9 worry in play as a fairness condition, not just a caution: if your friend declines even minimal, self-chosen, non-audited arrangements and offers no alternative, the privacy reading starts doing the work of the simpler reading — not wanting to participate — and you are entitled to notice that. Conversely, if an exposure-reducing arrangement is accepted and the peace holds, the privacy reading earns something.

Two things I am rejecting or re-timing. The account's recurrence test cannot confirm its hypothesis, for the objection's o2 reasons: falling recurrence is compatible with quieted resentment, displacement onto new items, or a lopsided arrangement with clearer paperwork. Keep the specification move; demote the test to weak evidence in every direction. And the spec note should not go into the group channel yet, on grounds the objection did not quite give: not evidential priority but feasibility. The withdrawing friend gates every group-level move, and a note drafted by two flatmates in the third's absence is the worst available move if legitimacy friction is live — it enacts the standing complaint. If you draft anything, either wait for all three or frame it from the start as a non-binding draft the absent friend can veto. This is also why the classification cross-check must stay a comparison of notes, not a formation of a front.

I decline the objection's reordering request in its original form (conversational form "first"), while granting its substance: orderings of hypotheses are cheap — any of the five readings could be put first — but orderings of moves should follow feasibility, and the avoider's participation is the feasibility constraint under every hypothesis.

On the eventual question — whether the living arrangement still fits — the account's step 5 and the rival's r11 converge on naming it rather than deferring it, and the objection worried the account left it too late. The fix is to pre-register the threshold now, privately: after two low-pressure one-to-one attempts at least a week apart, plus one no-strings offer, if your friend declines all engagement, offers no alternative, and the other flatmate confirms the withdrawal is general, the question has become the arrangement — raised as a conversation, not an ultimatum. Deciding the trigger in advance is what protects you from both indefinite deferral and forcing a lease conversation out of a chore dispute.

What stays open: which reading is true (only your observations can say), whether your friend's avoidance is warranted (nothing in any artifact settles that, and I have not either), and whether the flat works (gated behind the threshold). A last caution: you will run the retrospective classifier with an interpretation already in hand, and so will the other flatmate; that is why wording over gist, and why two independent classifications beat one. And if reading the rows above made one of them instantly recognizable — "that's exactly the fight we had" — trust the recognition over the apparatus. The selector has already done its work.
